title: Understanding Performance Collapse in Layer-Pruned Large Language Models via Decision Representation Transitions
claim: Layers split into a silent stage and a decisive stage; probing with iterative pruning exposes the collapse that one-shot pruning hides.
layout: 2 stacked rounded panels; top layer strips, bottom pruning-path graphs; dashed red transition line
description: Two stacked rounded panels. The top panel shows three horizontal strips of square blocks, one per layer: Dense LLM, Pruned LLM A and Pruned LLM B. Light green blocks mark the Silent Phase and dark green blocks mark the Decisive Phase. A dashed red vertical line, with a red-outlined block and a down arrow labeled Transition Point, separates the two phases. In the pruned strips some blocks are white, meaning those layers were removed. Pruned LLM B loses layers in the silent region, and its decisive blocks turn light green. The bottom panel contrasts Direct Prune with Iterative Pruning. In Direct Prune, a blue Dense LLM circle sends long arcs to five shrinking green pruned-model circles. In Iterative Pruning, a chain of short hops leads through a lightning-bolt Performance Drop. The eye goes first to the dark-green transition block and the red dashed line.
caption: (Top) Conceptual illustration of the Silent Phase and Decisive Phase as pruning rate increases. (Bottom) Comparison between traditional one-shot/global layer pruning frameworks and our proposed Iterative Pruning (IP) method, which acts as an analytical probe to track decision-level evolution.
abstract: Layer pruning efficiently reduces Large Language Model (LLM) computational costs but often triggers sudden performance collapse. Existing representation-based analyses struggle to explain this mechanism. We propose studying pruning through decision representation. Focusing on multiple-choice tasks, we introduce two metrics, Decision Margin and Option Frequency, and an Iterative Pruning method to analyze layer-wise decision dynamics. Our findings reveal a sharp decision transition that partitions the network into two stages: a Silent Phase, where the model cannot yet predict the correct answer, and a Decisive Phase, where the correct prediction emerges. We also find that pruning the Decisive Phase has minimal impact, whereas pruning the Silent Phase triggers immediate performance collapse, highlighting its extreme sensitivity to structural changes. Therefore, we conclude that pruning-induced collapse stems from disrupting the Silent Phase, which prevents the critical decision transition from occurring.
